catalog_quote: [1994: 20] Two-syllable words are common in Lotud, and the most common pattern is stress on the first syllable. All of the two syllable words in this conversation have the stress on the first syllable with the exception of pándán, which has equal stress on both syllables. This is typical of words with two closed syllables, such as mántád from a previous conversation. However, there are other common words which are stressed on the last syllable, hilú’ and kadái, for example. Though this is the pattern for elicited words, in the context of a sentence the stress on a word may shift to the final syllable, for instance for emphasis. In three-syllable words the stress is most commonly on the second from the last syllable, as you will see in the words mamátuw, momónsoi, and kadáyan. Other three-syllable words regularly have stress on both the first and last syllables, the stronger stress often…

new_statements.quote: There are twenty-two segmental phonemes in Lotud: eighteen consonants /p t k ʔ b d g s h dʒ m n ɲ ŋ l r w y/ and four vowels /i u a ɔ/. Stress is noncontrastive. [...] (p. 60) /tutubit/ [tu'tubit̪] 'castenet of priestess' ... /kadayan/ [kə'dayən] 'person' /sakɔt/ ['sakɔt̪] 'grass' ... (p. 61) /mɔgihum/ [mɔgi'hum] 'to look for' ... /natanan/ [ˌnatə'nan] 'all' ... (p. 62) /nɔkɔsiŋud/ [ˌnɔkə'siŋud] 'to have smelled' ... /a/ [ə] mid central unrounded vowel; occurs in unstressed syllables of words with three or more syllables: /mamanaw/ [ˌmamə'naw] 'to walk, go' /antadan/ [ˌʔantə'dan] 'honey bee'

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE CHECK. (Blood & Blood 1993 'Lotud phonemics', Sabah Museum Monograph 4, Rosetta scan of pp. 59-62 + title page). Rendered the page images (not just the garbled djvu text layer): p. 59 sec. 2 'Phonemes' reads exactly '...eighteen consonants /p t k ʔ b d g s h dʒ m n ɲ ŋ l r w y/ and four vowels /i u a ɔ/. Stress is noncontrastive.' The stress-marked forms the reader lists are all on pp. 60-62 as stated ([tu'tubɪt̚], [kə'dayən], ['sakɔt̚], [mə'ŋaki], [mɔgi'hum], [ˌnatə'nan], [ˌʔɪŋgərə'nan], [ʔi'nɔwit̚], [ˌnɔkə'sɪŋud], [ˌbino'kol], [ˌmamə'naw], [ˌʔantə'dan], [ˌʔɔsə'mɔk], [ˌmɔmə'lɔkɔŋ]; every disyllable penult-stressed; p. 62 [ə] 'occurs in unstressed syllables'). Reader's summary of that…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The authors state only that stress is not contrastive; the pages available (59-62) give no placement rule. Their stress-marked phonetic forms show penultimate stress in every disyllable and, in words of three or more syllables, primary stress on either the penult ([tu'tubit], [kə'dayən], [mə'ŋaki], [ʔi'nɔwit], [ˌnɔkə'siŋud], [ˌmɔmə'lɔkɔŋ]) or the final syllable ([mɔgi'hum], [ˌnatə'nan], [ˌmamə'naw], [ˌʔantə'dan], [ˌʔɔsə'mɔk], [ˌbino'kol], [ˌʔiŋgarə'nan]), i.e. a right-edge (penult~final) stress whose conditioning is not stated in the accessible pages; pp. 63-69 of the article (not scanned) may contain the rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed in the available pages, but transcriptions mark a secondary stress on the initial syllable of words of three or more syllables (e.g. [ˌnatə'nan], [ˌmamə'naw], [ˌnɔkə'siŋud], [ˌmɔmə'lɔkɔŋ], [ˌʔiŋgarə'nan]).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; unassimilated Malay loans keep Malay shape ([pər'tʃuma] 'free', ['tʃukup] 'enough'). Vowel reduction of /a/, /ɔ/ to [ə] is tied to unstressed syllables (p. 62).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms (isolated words elicited 1985-87 in Kg. Ro'un, Damat and Tutu, 'main dialect' of Lotud); no phrase-level discussion in the pages seen.
new_statements.identity_note: Blood & Blood 1993 describe what they call the 'main dialect' of Lotud (Kg. Ro'un, Damat and Tutu near Tuaran; also known as Dusun Tuaran) = Glottolog lotu1250, ISO dtr. Banker 1984 notes a second dialect, 'Dusun Kadayan' of Telipok/Sumagit, not covered by the phonemics paper. Lobel 2013 places Lotud in a Bisaya-Lotud subgroup rather than Dusunic proper.

sources.note: p. 59: 'Stress is noncontrastive.' No placement rule in the four pages scanned (pp. 63-69 missing). Stress-marked phonetic forms pp. 60-62: every disyllable penultimate (['sisip], ['papak], ['sakot], ['badi], ['sodop]...); trisyllables split between penult ([tu'tubit], [kə'dayən], [mə'ŋaki], [ʔi'nɔwit]) and final ([mɔgi'hum], [ˌnatə'nan], [ˌmamə'naw], [ˌʔantə'dan], [ˌʔɔsə'mɔk], [ˌbino'kol]); longer words [ˌnɔkə'siŋud], [ˌmɔmə'lɔkɔŋ] penult, [ˌʔiŋgarə'nan] final; secondary stress marked word-initially; /a/, /ɔ/ -> [ə] 'in unstressed syllables' (p. 62).
